# Benchmarks

<!-- Generated by `node scripts/benchmark.js` at 2026-10-16T09:23:53.403Z.
     Do not edit by hand: re-run the script and commit the result.

> **Read this first.** These are measurements of a *reference implementation* on
> a single small machine, running a test network with a handful of validators.
> They are not mainnet capacity, not a service-level commitment, not a promise
> about future versions, and not a comparison with any other chain. The
> protocol's throughput targets are in [SPEC.md](SPEC.md); what this file adds is
> evidence about what the current code actually does, with the hardware, the
> configuration and the workload named so that anyone can repeat it and get an
> answer they can check.

## 1. Command

```bash
node scripts/benchmark.js --validators 4 --block-time 1500 \
     --duration 90 --accounts 16 --concurrency 32 \
     --workload evm-write
```

Exit code is 0 only if the run completed, every included transaction is
confirmed, and the supply audit still balances afterwards.

## 4. Results

| Metric | Value | How it was measured |
|---|---|---|
| Transactions submitted | 948 | eth_sendRawTransaction calls this script made |
| Transactions included | 948 | a receipt was readable for the hash |
| Submissions refused | 0 | the node rejected the transaction at admission |
| Never included | 0 | accepted into the pool, no receipt inside the 10 s poll window |
| Sustained throughput | 10.5 tx/s | included transactions / wall-clock seconds of the measured window |
| Throughput per validator | 2.6 tx/s | the same figure divided by the validator count: every validator re-executes every block |
| Gas throughput | 239,490 gas/s | sum of block gasUsed / wall-clock seconds |
| Block utilisation | 0.28% of the block gas limit | mean block gasUsed / blockGasLimit |
| Block interval | mean 1,776 ms, p50 1,748 ms, p95 1,799 ms, max 3,035 ms | difference between consecutive block header timestamps |
| Transactions per block | mean 17.9, max 32 | length of the transactions array per block |
| Blocks produced | 52 over 90.6 s | heights observed inside the measured window |
| Latency to inclusion | p50 3,191 ms, p95 4,487 ms, p99 4,623 ms, max 4,663 ms | submit -> first readable receipt, polled every 50 ms |
| Finality | 1 block | a Full Stop block carries the precommits that sealed it, so a transaction is final in the block that includes it; there is no epoch to wait for |
| Consensus rounds | p50 0, max 1, 98.1% of blocks committed at round 0 | header.round per block; round > 0 means a view change happened |
| Cold node sync + replay | 58 blocks in 6.5 s = 9 blocks/s | an empty data directory, one peer, re-executed every block from genesis (the state trie is not persisted) |
| Sync agreement | identical state root and app hash at height 58 | both nodes asked for the same height and their headers compared: heads are not comparable while the chain advances |
| Chain size after the run | 459.3 KiB of blocks, 946 KiB of receipts | on-disk JSONL sizes of the RPC node store |
| RPC read latency | 12 ms mean, 33 ms p95 over 10 calls | fs_status + eth_getBlockByNumber pairs sampled between submissions |

## 6. Supply accounting after the run

A benchmark that makes the chain cheaper to use than it is safe would show up
here, because the same conservation assertion validators make at the end of each
block is re-run against the finished state.

| Supply check | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Hard cap | 100,000,000 LDX | a protocol constant, asserted on every mint |
| Issued | 75,000,005.8 LDX | sum of protocol mints since genesis |
| Burned | 0.0110434 LDX | fee burn plus slash burn; permanently removed |
| Unissued | 24,999,994.2 LDX | head-room left under the cap |
| Issued as % of cap | 75% | the cap is a ceiling, not a schedule |
| Conservation | holds: 75,000,005.788957 LDX on chain = 75,000,005.788957 LDX minted minus burned | the node walks the whole state trie and asserts sum(balances) === minted - burned |
| Staking escrow | exact: the module holds 20,000 LDX against 20,000 LDX of recorded bonds |


## 7. What these numbers do not say

- All 5 node processes shared 2 logical cores on one machine, so this run is CPU-bound and says nothing about a geographically distributed validator set.
- The state trie is not persisted by this implementation: a node re-executes the block log at start-up. The cold-node figure is therefore a combined sync *and* replay measurement, and start-up cost grows linearly with chain length (see docs/ADR.md).
- Throughput is bounded by single-threaded JavaScript execution and by the block gas limit. No parallel execution, no caching layer and no native (non-JVM/JS) runtime is part of this build.
- Every validator re-executes every transaction. Use "throughput per validator" when sizing hardware for a real set; the aggregate is the same work done N times in parallel.
- Not measured here, and not claimed: adversarial validators, wide-area network latency, disk contention under load, evidence submission storms, node restarts mid-block, long-range key reuse, or behaviour past 64 validators.
- The workload is evm-write. A transfer benchmark measures admission control and block packaging more than EVM throughput; run `--workload evm-write` for a write-heavy picture and report both.

## 8. Reproducing this

```bash
npm install                 # node >= 20
npm run compile             # system-contract artifacts the genesis is verified against
node scripts/benchmark.js    # writes this file and artifacts/benchmark-latest.json
node tools/determinism-check.js
npm test
```

The same script under a write-heavy workload is committed next to this file
(`docs/BENCHMARKS-EVM-WRITE.md`, produced by
`node scripts/benchmark.js --workload evm-write --report docs/BENCHMARKS-EVM-WRITE.md
--json artifacts/benchmark-evm-write.json`). Report both numbers together: the
transfer workload shows what admission control and consensus pacing cost, the
write workload shows what the EVM costs.

`artifacts/benchmark-latest.json` holds the raw per-transaction timings and every
block row, so each aggregate above can be recomputed from it. If your machine
produces different numbers, that is a real result too: publish it next to this
file rather than overwriting it.
